en: The *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Khararīṣi, relying upon the Ṛṣi Muni.

At the place where he dwelt, he was accompanied by an immeasurable great assembly of bhikṣus, as well as by an immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya number of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal to the sands of the Ganges River, all of whom had come from other buddha-fields in different directions.

At that time, the World-Honored One desired to preach for the great assembly the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra on the Four Eloquences, the Three Clarities, the Brahma-Conduct, and the Abiding that Destroys Evil Karmic Obstructions*.

At that time, to the west, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty Ganges Rivers, there was a buddha-field named *Sarvagandhasamuccayāśraya* (Abode of the Collection of All Fragrances), where the sentient beings had fully manifested the five turbidities.

In that land there is a Buddha named Śrīpuṣpadharagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; that Buddha is currently turning the sublime wheel of Dharma for the great assembly.
In that world, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Gaganagañja who, having heard the profound and wondrous Dharma from that Buddha, had attained various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).

At that time, the bodhisattva saw immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers of great bodhisattvas from other directions ascending into the air and proceeding toward the east. Furthermore, seeing a great radiance in the eastern world from afar, he immediately went to the presence of the Buddha Saṃkusumitarājendra, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

I saw immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of great bodhisattvas from other directions rising into the air and proceeding toward the eastern quarter; furthermore, I saw from afar a great radiance in the world-system of the east.
"By what causes and conditions does this matter arise?
I only pray that you will explain it to me in detail.
At that time, the Buddha Saṃkusumitarājendra addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:

“Good son! To the east of here, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-field named Sahā, where the sentient beings have come to possess the five corruptions.”

In that land there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He is currently at Mount Kālaṅgiri, dwelling in the abode of the Sage Muni, for the sake of ensuring that the flow of the Dharma remains uninterrupted;
for the sake of ensuring that the Three Jewels abide eternally in the world;
and for the sake of subduing all Māras and establishing the banner of the Dharma.
It is for the purpose of closing the gates of birth and death and opening the way to parinirvāṇa;

it is for the sake of the great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who have gathered to hear him preach the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra on the Four Eloquences, the Three Clarities, the Brahma-Conduct, Abiding, and the Destruction of Obstacles to Evil Karma*;

and it is because he wishes to cause all the bodhisattvas from the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Stage of Near-Perfection (*abhiṣeka-bhūmi*) in all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions—who abide in the unshared dharmas (*aveṇika-dharma*), do not rely on the faith of others, and are skilled in expedient means and endowed with unimpeded eloquence—such great beings as these, to gather like clouds; for these reasons, that Buddha has emitted this light.

When those bodhisattvas had seen this light, they traveled through the air to that degenerate age and preached for the sake of all sentient beings the *dhāraṇī* for destroying the obstacles of evil karma.
That Buddha-land also possesses the five turbidities, being no different from this world.

You should now go to the Sahā world to pay homage, make offerings, and listen to the True Dharma; furthermore, for the sake of the evil sentient beings in that land, you should preach the *Dhāraṇī for Destroying Evil Karmic Obstructions*.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja was filled with joy and exultation; together with eight billion bodhisattvas, he simultaneously raised his voice and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now thirst for and long to see that Buddha; I shall now, relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, proceed to the Sahā world to the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha, where I will pay homage, behold him, make offerings, and listen to the True Dharma, and also preach the *Dhāraṇī for Destroying Evil Karmic Obstructions* for the sake of the various evil sentient beings in that land.
Then the Buddha Padmavṛṣabhavikrāmin replied to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You yourself know the proper time.”
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha, together with eight billion bodhisattvas, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and ascended into the air, proceeding toward the Sahā world.
At that time, a light from a wish-fulfilling jewel appeared in the western direction, surrounded by immeasurable śakrābhilagna jewels.

The radiance of that jewel eclipsed all the light of the eight classes of gods and humans, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, as well as the light of the realms of earth, water, fire, and wind, such that none of them appeared again.

At that time, the great assembly beheld only the Buddha’s light and the light of the jewels—immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and ineffable; there were no other colors remaining, and they saw only empty space.

At that time, the Tathāgata’s radiant light shone so brightly that the great assembly could not see themselves nor one another; all forms were extinguished without remainder and did not confront the eyes. They could not perceive their own physical characteristics or appearances, and regarding what was touched, there was neither "that" nor "this," nor anything in between. In whichever direction they looked, it was exactly like this.
Furthermore, he did not see the sun, moon, or stars, nor the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind; none of these appeared before his eyes.

His ears heard no sounds, his nose smelled no fragrances, his tongue perceived no tastes, and his body felt no tactile sensations. Among the various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), there was nothing upon which to focus. He no longer gave rise to notions of "self" or "mine," nor did he have any conceptualization regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). He could not perceive the great elements or the vast assembly that had gathered; he saw only the light of the Buddha and the light of the jewel, which was surrounded by immeasurable *śakrābhilagna* gems.

Among those in the assembly, the great bodhisattvas who had attained the ten stages, who had realized the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, and who were in their final birth before buddhahood—upon seeing this sign, their bodies and minds became peaceful and stable, neither startled nor terrified.

Why is this? It is because they have realized the true nature of the characteristics of phenomena through their understanding, and because they abide in suchness and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

However, when the other bodhisattvas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, non-humans, and others saw these signs, they were struck with terror and confusion; their minds became agitated, they could no longer see one another, nor was there anyone to ask for guidance. They thought to themselves:
"Unknowing what cause has brought about these extraordinary signs,
and likewise not knowing whose spiritual power they are," at that time,
among the assembly there was a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva named Brahmakūṭa. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and spoke in verse:
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena—sentient beings are ignorant of this;
bound and attached to the aggregate of form, they are deluded by the six sense faculties.
Failing to see even a single aggregate, they pursue and seek out the aggregate of form."
Having conceived doubts regarding the Buddha-dharma,
I pray that you will expound the definitive teaching, so as to sever the web of all doubts,
enable us to know both this shore and the other, and cause us to attain the patience of space.
The valiant one enters samādhi; his physical marks are ineffable.
A great wish-fulfilling jewel is always upon his crown, surrounded by Śakrābhilagna gems.
The great beings in this assembly, all of whom occupy the rank of the ten stages,
who have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and are in their final birth before Buddhahood— all these bodhisattvas behold him from afar.
Having beheld this auspicious sign, one knows for certain that a supreme being has arrived;

having paid homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One, he shall preach the profound and wondrous Dharma to comfort sentient beings who are terrified, as they take refuge in the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
"The sphere of action for the courageous is to teach and mature sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Excellent, just as you have said; this is the sphere of action for those established in meditative concentration."
The physical form is invisible, yet cultivated wisdom can investigate it.
This is the Abode of Space, the place where he always dwells;
free from dependence and conceptual proliferation, it is manifested through the power of samādhi.
Sentient beings are attached to two views and are constantly deluded by them;
because of that delusion, they do not know this shore or the other shore.
Desiring to leave behind these two views, one should cultivate the practice that is ineffable.
They swiftly attain the ultimate goal and fulfill all the stages (*bhūmi*).
"Furthermore, good son,

a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment should practice the six *pāramitās* by means of the characteristics of initial resolve and the characteristics of objective referents, until they know, in accordance with reality, the nature of the arising and ceasing of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness."
Furthermore, one knows that all phenomena are ineffable, devoid of intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, free from objective referents, unmoving and unshakable, empty and non-existent.

Practicing all dharmas in this manner, one remains free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism and does not give rise to fear. One does not produce the perception of contact regarding any dharma; the mind is without攀缘 (ālambana) and is empty and non-existent. Practicing in this way, one swiftly fulfills the six pāramitās and no longer dwells within the views of annihilationism and eternalism.

When the Tathāgata spoke these words, the entire assembly saw, heard, perceived, and cognized them as they truly appeared in their original form and color, yet they did not grasp at the signs within those objects.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right hand, pointed toward the western direction, and spoke these words:
"Such an auspicious omen of light is a sign that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha is about to arrive."

This bodhisattva possesses all samādhis like the great ocean; abides in the bodhisattva precepts like Mount Sumeru; has a mind of forbearance like a diamond; is as vigorous and courageous as a swift wind; possesses wisdom like space and insight like the sands of the Ganges.
Among all bodhisattvas, he is like a great and victorious banner; he is the Great Teacher leading toward parinirvāṇa, the ground of roots of goodness.

He is a jar of auspiciousness for the poor, a sun for those in darkness, a moon for those who have lost their way, a place of refuge for those in fear, nectar-water for the parching heat of afflictions, and [the support] for those with roots of goodness.

It is a staff, a bridge to parinirvāṇa, a ladder for those ascending to heaven, a boat for crossing saṃsāra, a vehicle for traversing the vast wilderness, and a parasol for those scorched by the heat of slander and harsh speech.
It subdues all non-Buddhists like a lion, purifies all views like rainwater, and destroys the enemies of affliction like a thunderbolt; it shatters the violation of precepts.
This medicine is like a springtime rain for sprouting the shoots of wholesome roots;
it is like a floral garland for adorning Bodhisattvas; it is like a bright mirror for revealing good and evil conduct; it is like exquisite clothing for those lacking shame and remorse;

it is a great and excellent physician for those afflicted by the three sufferings; it is like a moon-pearl for those who are parched with heat and thirst; and it is for those who are utterly exhausted...
It is a couch;

it is like a sun-gem for all samādhis, a great ox-cart for the path to bodhi, a cool lotus pond for those who roam in dhyāna and samādhi, and the fruit of the pāramitās that adorns the garland of bodhi. It is the wish-fulfilling maṇi within the ten stages, and the pārijātaka tree for those seeking the śūraṅgama-samādhi.
The sword that fells evil views severs the habitual tendencies of afflictions like a vajra;
it subdues all māras and gives rise to a treasury of merit and wisdom, relying upon the virtues of all Buddhas.

This is the cave-dwelling relied upon by all pratyekabuddhas; it is the eye of the śrāvakas and the eye of those born in the heavens; it is the straight path for those traveling on deviant ways; it is the refuge for animals and hungry ghosts; and it is the salvation for those in the hells.

The unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings, the foremost minister of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, capable of protecting the city of the Dharma, who has already perfected the eighteen unique qualities of the secret treasury of all Buddhas, who has fully realized and accomplished the wisdom of a Buddha, and who is worthy of offerings from all devas and humans—save for the Tathāgata himself, none can equal him.

"All of you in this great assembly should, with deep sincerity and reverence, welcome the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja. According to your respective capacities, you should honor and make offerings to him with various adornments such as exquisite jeweled banners, streamers, parasols, flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, robes, bedding, songs, hymns, and praises, as well as by leveling and clearing the roads."
"You, the great assembly, should all likewise become vessels for such merit.

At that time, the great assembly rose from their seats and, toward the direction where the auspicious sign had appeared before the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, they leaped for joy with cheerful countenances; with eyes fixed in rapt attention, they together went forth to welcome him.

The other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and great śrāvakas, as well as the lords of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and the lords of the rishis with five supernatural powers, each had this thought:
"What most supreme and exquisite offerings should we prepare to make an offering to that Great Being?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, by means of his supernormal powers, transformed the Sahā world, removing all impurities and evils, as well as hills, mountains, tiles, rubble, thorns, pits, mounds, wildernesses, and narrow passes. The wind, dust, clouds, and mist were all completely cleared away; the ground became composed of the seven treasures, level as the palm of a hand, with immeasurable varieties of precious jewels forming its groves and trees. The branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were all made of jewels, and the same was true for the famous blossoms and soft grasses, their fragrant scents wafting powerfully throughout the world.

All sentient beings within the Sahā world shall be free from all suffering and affliction; blindness, deafness, muteness, lameness, and all manner of ailments shall be cured simultaneously. Those who harbor enmity and malice shall all give rise to hearts of compassion. The sounds of agony in the hells and among the hungry ghosts shall all cease, and food, drink, clothing, and articles of adornment shall naturally become abundant and sufficient.

Those sentient beings possess wondrous and upright forms with all limbs and joints complete, and their majestic virtue is supreme; having eliminated all fetters and afflictions, their minds attain tranquility; they take deep delight in the roots of goodness and abide in the Three Jewels with pure faith.

The entire assembly each held a wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewel in both hands; from within these jewels issued forth great radiance that illuminated the entire world, while celestial music was played. A rain of various kinds of jewels and multicolored precious robes fell, as well as a rain of various exquisite ornaments, jeweled garlands, jeweled canopies, various precious vessels, various celestial garments, golden chains, necklaces of pearls, and blue, red, crimson, and white lotuses of variegated colors. Furthermore, a rain of *agaru* incense and *gośīrṣa* sandalwood fell, filling the entire world.
On both sides of that road were seven-jeweled terraces like the palaces of Śakra.

Furthermore, within those terraces, celestial maidens filled them to capacity; their countenances were dignified and beautiful, resembling those of the Queen of Māra, as they performed divine music producing the five tones.
Furthermore, above the Buddha, a great Brahmā-king’s canopy made of the seven celestial jewels was suspended in mid-air as an offering to the Tathāgata.

This canopy was a hundred thousand yojanas in circumference and was further covered by a net of jewels. Tassels of pearl streamers hung down as ornaments on all four sides. From within the canopy issued various musical sounds, pure, subtle, harmonious, and elegant, surpassing those of both humans and devas.

All the great earth, its grasses, trees, forests, flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves all produced wondrous sounds, proclaiming and expounding the practices of the various stages and the six pāramitās of the Mahāyāna.
Those who heard his voice all became non-retrogressive regarding the unsurpassed path, and some even attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the great assembly, witnessing the extraordinary and marvelous supernatural transformations of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, felt joy in their hearts and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Each thought to themselves: "Since this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has manifested such great supernormal powers, he will surely come to this world before long."
"What kind of seats should we now prepare to wait upon him?

While this thought arose among the assembly, a precious lotus flower immediately sprang up from the earth before the Buddha. It had a stem of white silver, leaves of gold, a pedestal of diamond, a pericarp of lapis lazuli, filaments of agate, the bases of the filaments made of Brahma-colored jewels, and anthers of crystal. The flower was one hundred *yojanas* in height and breadth, surrounded on all sides by eight billion precious lotus flowers.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha suddenly appeared upon that precious lotus flower and sat cross-legged; furthermore, a wish-fulfilling jewel was seen atop his head, surrounded by immeasurable śākalmaṇi gems, while eight billion bodhisattvas each sat upon other precious lotus flowers.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva spoke these verses to question Bhaisajyarāja Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
"Since the distant past, I have seen multitudes of bodhisattvas who,
coming to visit the World-Honored One, first circumambulated him with reverence."
Having performed the prostration by touching the head to the feet, he then withdrew and took his seat.
How is it that this Great Being manifests such supernatural power,
sitting upon a precious lotus flower without observing the customary rites of a bodhisattva?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja replied in verse:
“This man of great wisdom, Well-established in the profound and wondrous Dharma,
Not relying on a mind of deluded conceptualization, Has come to see the World-Honored One.”
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again asked in verse:
"If one does not perceive sentient beings, Nor the characteristics of any phenomena,
And one's mind always dwells in peace Within the true reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of all phenomena,"
"How do you manifest the power of sovereign supernormal faculties?
We pray that you will explain this for us, to dispel our doubts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja replied in verse:
"Now this Great Being, valiant and skilled in means,
manifests this supernatural power for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
If he did not abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), [he would be no different from] deluded ordinary folk."
"The wise open the way to conventional truth for the sake of entering ultimate truth.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! It is as you have said.
All ordinary sentient beings cannot fathom the sphere of liberation and conduct of even a single srotāpanna."
All sentient beings who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* cannot fathom the sphere of liberation and practice of even a single *sakṛdāgāmin*;
all sentient beings who have attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* cannot fathom the sphere of liberation and practice of even a single *anāgāmin*;
all sentient beings who have attained the stage of *anāgāmin* cannot fathom the sphere of liberation and practice of even a single *arhat*.
All sentient beings, even if they were to become arhats, could not conceive of the sphere of liberation and conduct of a single pratyekabuddha;

all sentient beings, even if they were to become pratyekabuddhas, could not conceive of the sphere of skillful means and conduct of a single bodhisattva mahāsattva associated with the *prajñāpāramitā* who matures sentient beings;

all sentient beings, even if they were to attain the sphere of skillful means and conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva associated with the *prajñāpāramitā* who matures sentient beings, could not fathom the sphere of skillful means and conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), nor their manner of lifting and setting down the feet, nor how they mature sentient beings by realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

All sentient beings who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) cannot fathom the skillful means and spheres of activity of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and bring sentient beings to maturity; nor can they fathom the skillful means and spheres of activity of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who possess the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), raise and lower their feet with skillful means, understand the ultimate truth, and bring sentient beings to maturity.

All sentient beings who possess the four analytical knowledges cannot fathom the skillful means and spheres of activity of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who abide in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) and the ultimate Śūraṅgama Samādhi, raise and lower their feet with skillful means, understand the ultimate truth, and bring sentient beings to maturity.

“Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has, throughout immeasurable kalpas, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and perfected unimpeded eloquence. He has reached the ultimate fulfillment of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and dwells on the supreme stage with decisive firmness, never to be shaken. He thoroughly knows the deep inclinations and actions of sentient beings and should manifest the adornments of divine transformations for them. Furthermore, seeing the auspicious signs that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha intends to arrive, and seeing that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has attained the stage of freedom from desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*), the stage of abiding (*vihāra-bhūmi*), and the stage of entry (*praveśa-bhūmi*), he has manifested the entry into the *ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi* and vanished in the western direction to appear here.”

At that time, because all sentient beings were terrified and deluded, they entered into conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); [the Buddha] manifested great adornments for the sake of bringing those sentient beings to maturity.
Furthermore, noble son!

If this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha manifests the adornment of non-arising according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all devas, humans, and even Bodhisattvas up to the eighth stage will become bewildered and distressed; none will be able to perceive the characteristics of his sphere or his conduct, for he has skillfully entered such profound and wondrous merit.

“Good son! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has, through his skillful means and wisdom, entered deeply into the ocean of all Buddhas’ teachings. Because he is free from all doubt and does not rely on others, his skillful wisdom is the supreme king of banners among all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.”

“Good son! The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is the great enlightened guide for all sentient beings seeking rebirth in heaven or parinirvāṇa; he is able to sever all afflictions and mental ailments, and skillfully treats the poisons of the body as well as diseases of the four great elements.”

If there are sentient beings who give rise to evil and false views, they will wander and sink in the wilderness of birth and death, lacking skillful means and thus ignorant of the path to rebirth in heaven or to parinirvāṇa.

If there are sentient beings who invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja and take refuge in him with a sincere heart, burning solid black aloeswood and tagara incense while performing respectful prostrations, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja observes the roots of goodness within the minds of these sentient beings.

If one sees sentient beings deluded and distracted by various views and afflictions; or if one sees the seeds of past roots of goodness, the mental activities, and the deeds performed, including their capacity for giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and other virtues directed toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha observed those sentient beings and, manifesting various forms within their dreams according to how they should be perceived, he taught them the Dharma through skillful means.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who should perceive the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja through awakening, they shall immediately see his various forms before their eyes. Thereupon, by means of skillful expedients, he opens the straight path for them, shattering the evil karma, false views, evil vows, evil refuges, evil destinations, and evil graspings of all sentient beings. He causes those who are thus attached to be completely liberated; their actions of body, speech, and mind become free from all crookedness, as they proceed toward the straight path, right action, right view, right vow, right refuge, right destination, and right grasp. They constantly gain proximity to virtuous spiritual friends, swiftly abandon the fetters of foul afflictions, and forever escape the sufferings of the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties. Constantly performing wholesome deeds, they attain the power of mastery, and even gradually enter into profound *dharmakṣānti*.”

If there are sentient beings who suffer from various physical ailments, or whose minds are deranged, or who are deaf, blind, mute, or have crippled hands and feet such that their sense faculties are incomplete—if they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, take refuge in him with a sincere heart, burn solid black aloeswood and tagara incense, and pay respectful homage, whether seeking medicine or wishing for recovery—[they shall be healed].
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha immediately manifested according to their wishes:
appearing in the form of Brahmā, or appearing in the form of Śakra Devendra, or appearing in the form of Vaiśravaṇa,
or appearing in the form of the Four Heavenly Kings, or appearing in the form of Yama, or appearing in the form of Tuṣita, or appearing in his own [form].
He may manifest in the form of a celestial being, or manifest in the form of Maheśvara, or manifest in the form of a brahmin,
or manifest in the form of a kṣatriya, or manifest in the form of an elder, or manifest in the form of a householder, or manifest in the form of a minister or official,
or manifest in the form of a boy or a girl, or manifest in the form of parents or relatives.
Sometimes manifesting as the form of Vajrapāṇi, or manifesting as the forms of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—
manifesting such various forms before those who are dreaming and those who are awake.
He explains the characteristics of the illnesses and further distinguishes the various medicinal remedies for them:
"When the symptoms of illness are such as these, one should take this medicine; if the illness is of such a kind, it is appropriate to take that medicine."
Once all these sentient beings had heard this teaching, each prepared the various medicines according to their specific needs; if they lacked any themselves, the Bodhisattva provided them all.

Some of these beings were cured of all their ailments after taking one, two, or three doses, while others found their illnesses immediately eliminated simply by seeing the manifested body of the Bodhisattva.
Thus it is, noble son!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha is endowed with great compassion;
if there are sentient beings who are impoverished and suffering, desiring great wealth, desiring to recite and study extensively, desiring to delight in much learning, or desiring to seek liberation—
Desiring to be free from desire; desiring meditative concentration; desiring fame; desiring preeminence; desiring skillfulness; desiring mastery; desiring physical beauty; desiring a fine complexion;
desiring an exquisite voice; desiring a pleasant fragrance; desiring superior flavors; desiring a pleasant tactile sensation.
Desiring food and drink; desiring to seek valor and strength; desiring to obtain a noble lineage;
desiring to pray for the birth of a son or praying to seek a daughter; desiring to obtain a retinue; desiring to seek merit and virtue;
desiring to achieve the six pāramitās; desiring to obtain eloquence; and desiring to seek the protection and shelter of all sentient beings.
Those who wish to escape from all prisons and sever all evil vows, and who possess a mind of generosity, should establish themselves therein; this applies likewise even to wisdom.

Desiring long life; desiring abundant wealth so that, once obtained, it may be used effectively; wishing to cause the stingy to practice generosity; causing those who violate the precepts to firmly uphold the moral discipline; causing those who are wrathful to cultivate patience; causing those who are indolent to abide in diligence; instructing those with distracted minds to cultivate meditative concentration; causing those who are ignorant to cultivate wisdom; encouraging those not fixed in a vehicle to study the Śrāvaka vehicle; and teaching the Pratyekabuddha vehicle to sentient beings who are attached to a self.

If there are sentient beings who, being devoid of great compassion, cherish only their own bodies and abandon all other beings, may they resolve to leave such thoughts behind and give rise to great compassion; may they no longer protect themselves but instead embrace all sentient beings, and may they bring forth the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Good son! At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha, having known their thoughts, immediately manifested skillful means to cause these sentient beings to abandon their former intentions and give rise to great compassion. He caused them to no longer protect their own bodies and not to forsake sentient beings, so that they might resolve upon bodhicitta and abide in the four Brahma-vihāras."

If there are sentient beings who delight in great compassion, who wish to seek the salvation and relief of all sentient beings, and who aspire to abide securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should—whether in a forest hermitage, within a grove, or in an open space—burn solid black aloeswood and tagara incense; then, with palms joined in reverence toward the ten directions, they should prostrate themselves fully upon the ground and take refuge with a sincere heart.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja then spoke this dhāraṇī mantra:
“Amṛśa amṛśa | Kāruṇika | Ccara ccara vicara vicara sanvicara | Kāruṇika rama rama rumu” ||
The same applies to the following:

Kāṭali-ma-mukha (the *ma* is pronounced with the *qù* tone; the *mukha* is pronounced with the *qù* tone), Pūruṣavaka (the *va* is pronounced with the *bù* tone), Nakalunika, Cintāmaṇi-puraya-kalunika-sattva (the *sattva* is pronounced with the *dù* tone;

the same applies to the following), Śame (pronounced with the *mò* tone; read with the Wú accent), Tappaya, Añjate (the *añja* is pronounced with the *ér* tone), and Dhṛti-buddhi (the *buddhi* is pronounced with the *pǔ* tone).
...kṣaṇe kṣaṇe *kṣaṇe* (the *kṣaṇe* below is pronounced with the *qian* and *ju* radicals reversed;

the same applies to all subsequent instances), *pūṭi*, *kṣaṇarati* (the *rati* below is pronounced *duli*; the same applies to all subsequent instances), *vibhītakṣaṇe*, *tṛṣṭivibhītakṣaṇe*, *garuḍanikā* (the *nikā* is pronounced *fǎjiǔ*), *riyadruma* (the *druma* is pronounced *mùzuǒ*), *aśvakasattvapāli* (the *aśva* is pronounced *shǐjiā*; the *sattva* is pronounced *bǎolǐ*), *pakṣaya-aśoka* (the *aśoka* is pronounced *jūzuǒ*), *ga* (pronounced *jùzuǒ*), *ti svāhā*. "O Son of Good Family!..."

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha may manifest in the form of a deity, or appear as a human; he may take the form of a deer or a bird, or remain invisible. According to what is appropriate for each being, he employs various skillful means to preach the Dharma, thereby transforming and delivering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings, causing them to abide in the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, within a short time, they establish sentient beings so that they abide in the Mahāyāna and attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), even leading them to attain various profound samādhis and dhāraṇīs, and to fulfill the ten stages (bhūmi).

"Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha is endowed with great compassion. Even if one were able to conceive of the limits of space through contemplation, no one could measure the limits of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha’s wisdom, skillful means, great kindness, great compassion, and the power of his samādhi in maturing sentient beings."
"Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has accomplished such inconceivable merit and wisdom. Good son!"

If there are sentient beings whose minds are free from flattery and crookedness, as well as illusion and hypocrisy; whose minds are pure and sincere, entering the true stream; who perceive reality as it is; who do not criticize the shortcomings of others nor boast of themselves; who do not disparage others and remain free from all envy; who do not manifest themselves as extraordinary to deceive or delude the masses; and whose minds are fundamentally complete.

“Good son! Out of compassion for these sentient beings, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha, through the wisdom of skillful means and courageous diligence, cultivates virtuous expedients to eliminate the transgressions of these beings, cause them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and dedicate all their roots of goodness toward supreme enlightenment, so that they may attain non-retrogression and acquire great power as well as the power of diligence.”
In order to fulfill the six pāramitās,
they constantly and diligently cultivate great loving-kindness and great compassion, until finally attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has accomplished such inconceivable merit and virtue, and he courageously brings all sentient beings to fulfillment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what cause and condition does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja alone have this exquisite wish-fulfilling jewel upon the crown of his head, surrounded by immeasurable śakrābhilagna jewels, its brilliant radiance outshining all other colors, unlike those of the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha is endowed with great compassion and is able to rescue sentient beings from peril, distress, and danger."

If there are sentient beings who have committed root offenses and should fall into the evil realms, whose all roots of goodness have been utterly incinerated—then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja is the pure, radiant sun for the darkness of great ignorance and false views;
he is the great and excellent teacher who extinguishes root offenses;
he is able to extract the arrow of doubt and restore those who have shattered the vessel of the Dharma so that it is made whole once more.

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who have committed a pārājika offense, whose roots of goodness are severed, who are headed for hell, who have no refuge and are abandoned by the wise—if one can rescue and deliver them all, reveal the true path to them, and wash away the foul afflictions of sentient beings so that they may leave the evil realms—this is the ladder for ascending to the human and celestial realms and attaining liberation."

If there are sentient beings who, deluded by greed and confusion, can be awakened from their state; those whose minds are filled with anger and malice, or shrouded in the darkness of ignorance; those who slander the law of cause and effect, being heedless, faithless, and fearful of the future; those who greedily seek without satiety and harbor extreme jealousy, fully possessing the ten unwholesome karmas that increase day and night—[for these, one should apply the appropriate remedy].

For such sentient beings, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja is able to eliminate the aforementioned grave karmic offenses and establish them securely in the state of liberation among humans and devas, like a great chariot.
“Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha is one whom all devas, humans, and worldlings should respect, welcome, and make offerings to.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by committing a root offense, a *pārājika*?

If there are sentient beings who commit such an offense, their roots of goodness are incinerated; they fall into the evil realms and are separated from places of peace and security, forever losing all the joys of gods and humans.”
"This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha is able to cause these various evil sentient beings to once again attain the full abundance of the blessings and joys of humans and devas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:

“Good son! If a consecrated Kṣatriya king who possesses sovereign power commits the five root transgressions, all that he has previously cultivated will be utterly consumed by fire; he will lose his place of peace and security, depart from the joys of humans and devas, and fall into the evil destinies.”
What are called the five root offenses?
Good son, they are as follows:

a consecrated Kṣatriya king who possesses sovereign power over a kingdom takes the property of a stūpa or the property of the Saṅgha from the four quarters, or instructs others to take it; this is called committing the first root offense.
Furthermore, good son!

A consecrated Kṣatriya king who possesses sovereign power over his realm may slander the True Dharma, abandon the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Anuttara-yāna, and furthermore prohibit others from practicing and studying them; this is called the second root offense.
Furthermore, son of good family!

An anointed Kṣatriya king who possesses sovereign power over a kingdom, if he—on account of the Tathāgata—causes someone who has shaved off his beard and hair and donned the dharma-robes, whether that person maintains the precepts or violates them, whether they possess the precepts or lacks them—to strip away their kāṣāya robe and compel them to return to lay life; or if he inflicts flogging, or binds them, or cuts off their hands and feet, even unto taking their life; whether acting himself or inciting others to create such evil, this is called the third root offense.
Furthermore, good son!
An anointed Kṣatriya king who rules over a kingdom possesses sovereign power; yet he may commit the five heinous crimes. What are these five?
First, killing one's mother;
second, harming one's father;
third, killing an arhat.
Fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
fifth, shedding the blood of a Buddha.
If one commits even one of these five ānantarya crimes, it is called a violation of the root precepts; this is termed the fourth violation of the root precepts.
Furthermore, good son!

An anointed Kṣatriya king who rules over a kingdom possesses sovereign power; yet he slanders cause and effect, has no fear of the future, commits the ten paths of unwholesome action, and also teaches others to practice these ten evils. This is called the fifth root offense.
"Good son! These are called the five root offenses of a consecrated kṣatriya.

If one commits even one of them, it is termed a pārājika offense; all previously cultivated roots of goodness are utterly consumed by fire, one is separated from the state of peace and security, loses the happiness of humans and devas, and falls into the evil realms."

"Good son! For the sake of this person, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha gives rise to great compassion and manifests birth in a borderland region. According to what is appropriate for them to see, he manifests various forms—whether in the likeness of a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a householder, or a layman—and for their sake, he expounds the profound Mahāyāna dharma of the unexcelled omniscience, as well as various dhāraṇīs and the stages of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi). By means of such diverse and wondrous dharmas, he guides them."

Once the consecrated kṣatriya had heard the Dharma, he felt shame and remorse, and being filled with extreme fear, he confessed and repented before the teacher of the Dharma. Vowing never again to commit the offenses previously committed, he established himself in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; he diligently cultivated loving-kindness and compassion, giving rise to the happiness of humans and devas and the bliss of parinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A minister also has five root offenses that constitute a *pārājika*.

If one commits such an offense, all previously cultivated roots of goodness will be utterly consumed by fire; one will fall into the evil realms, departing from the place of peace and security, and will forever lose all the joys of gods and humans."
What are these five? They are as follows:

when a high minister governs the realm and, relying on the king's power, takes for himself the property of a stūpa or the property of the Saṃgha from the four directions, or instructs others to take it—this is called committing the first root offense.
Furthermore, good son!
If that minister, while governing the realm, relies upon the king’s power to destroy villages, towns, cities, or the country—or incites others to do so—this is called the second root offense.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If a high minister who governs the land relies upon the power of the king to slander the True Dharma, abandoning the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Anuttara-yāna, and furthermore restraining others so that they do not practice or study them, this is called the third root offense.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If a high minister who governs the land relies upon the power of the king, and seeing someone for the sake of the Tathāgata—whether that person has shaved off their hair and beard and wears the dharma robes, whether they observe the precepts or violate them, and whether they possess the precepts or not—he strips them of their *kāṣāya*, compels them to return to lay life, or inflicts flogging, or binds them, or cuts off their hands and feet, even up to taking their life; whether he does this himself or causes others to do so, such an evil act is called the fourth root offense.
Furthermore, good son!
If that minister governs the land by relying on the king’s power and commits the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*). What are these five?
First, killing one's mother;
second, harming one's father;
third, killing an arhat;
Fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
fifth, shedding the blood of a Buddha.
If one commits even one of these five crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), it is termed a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*); this is called the fifth fundamental offense.
"Good son! These are called the five root offenses of a great minister.

If one commits even one of them, this is termed a *pārājika* offense; all previously cultivated roots of goodness are utterly consumed by fire, one is separated from the state of security, loses the bliss of humans and devas, and falls into the evil realms."

“Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha, out of great compassion for this person, manifests birth in a frontier land. According to what each should see, he manifests various forms—whether as the likeness of a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a householder, or a lay devotee—and for their sake, he expounds the profound Mahāyāna Dharma of the unexcelled omniscience, the various dhāraṇīs, and the stages of patience. By means of such diverse and wondrous teachings, he guides them.”

At that time, having heard the Dharma, the minister felt shame and remorse and was filled with extreme fear. He confessed and repented before the teacher of the Dharma, vowing never again to commit the offenses he had previously committed. He established himself in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; he diligently cultivated loving-kindness and compassion, and gave rise to the happiness of humans and devas as well as the bliss of parinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Śrāvakas also have five root offenses that constitute a pārājika.

Should one commit such an offense, all previously cultivated roots of goodness will be utterly consumed by fire; one will fall into the evil destinies, depart from the state of peace and security, and lose the bliss of humans and devas."
What are these five? They are:
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and shedding the blood of a Buddha. Good son!
These are called the five root offenses of the śrāvakas.

If one commits even one of them, it is termed a pārājika offense; all previously cultivated roots of goodness are utterly consumed by fire, one is separated from the state of peace, loses the bliss of humans and devas, and falls into the evil destinies.

"Good son! For the sake of this person, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha gives rise to great compassion and manifests birth in a frontier land. According to what should be seen, he manifests various forms—whether in the likeness of a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a householder, or a lay devotee—and for their sake, he expounds the profound Mahāyāna Dharma of all-knowledge, the unprecedented dhāraṇīs, and the stages of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi). By means of such various sublime teachings, he guides them."

At that time, having heard the Dharma, those śrāvakas felt shame and remorse, and being filled with extreme terror, they confessed their transgressions to the teacher of the Dharma. Vowing never again to commit the offenses previously committed, they dwelt securely in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they diligently cultivated loving-kindness and compassion, giving rise to the happiness of humans and devas and the bliss of parinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, noble son!

For a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment and is progressing toward the Mahāyāna, there are eight root offenses that constitute pārājika transgressions. These completely incinerate all roots of goodness previously cultivated; one falls into evil realms, departs from places of peace and security, and loses the bliss of humans and devas. One also forfeits the bliss of the Mahāyāna sphere and remains for a long time in saṃsāra, far removed from virtuous friends."
What are these eight? They are as follows:

that bodhisattva, due to the causal conditions of past karma, is born in an age of the five turbidities; yet, possessing residual roots of goodness, they draw near to spiritual friends and take refuge in the profound Dharma of the Mahāyāna, while giving rise to the unsurpassed resolve with wisdom that is still slight and shallow.

When a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment hears from others the profound teaching of emptiness, reads, recites, and upholds it, yet subsequently reads, recites, and explains it before people of little wisdom and dull faculties; and when those others, having heard it, become startled, doubtful, and terrified, thereby falling away from the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and taking pleasure in the Śrāvaka vehicle—this is called the first root grave offense of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment. All the roots of goodness previously cultivated are completely incinerated; he falls into evil destinies and is separated from the state of peace and security; he loses the bliss of humans and devas as well as the bliss of the Mahāyāna realm, and his bodhicitta is destroyed.

Therefore, a bodhisattva should first know the roots of goodness of sentient beings and understand their minds, then teach the Dharma in successive stages according to what they can bear, just as one enters the great ocean by gradually reaching its depths.

“Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha manifests in various forms according to what is appropriate for those beings, appearing in their lands to preach the Dharma. He causes them to give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, so that they may confess and repent for the transgressions they have committed. Thus, they shall not fall into the evil realms and will instead advance their roots of goodness, nurturing the mind set on Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

"Good son! Furthermore, if a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind commits a root offense and, fearing falling into the evil destinies, hears the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja and, with a sincere heart, wishes to see him in order to confess and repent for the offenses committed, they should, during the final watch of the first part of the night, burn solid black aloeswood and tagara incense, join their palms with a sincere heart, and invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja."

"Good son! At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha manifests various forms according to what is appropriate—whether manifesting his own body, or the body of a śrāvaka, or the body of a kṣatriya or a brāhmaṇa, or even the bodies of boys, girls, and so forth—and appears before those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds but have committed offenses, instructing them to confess, repent, and eliminate their transgressions."

By means of skillful expedients, they reveal the stages of samādhi, dhāraṇī, and patience within the profound, unsurpassed, and truly correct Mahāyāna practice; they cause others to abandon all evil destinies, attain the non-retrogressive mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and diligently cultivate the six *pāramitās* until their power becomes as firm and solid as a vajra, even unto their own attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja does not manifest his body before that person to instruct them on confession, then that bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind should, during the final watch of the night, join their palms with a sincere heart and face the east. They should burn solid black aloeswood and tagara incense and address the Morning Star, saying:

"Morning Star, Morning Star, you who have perfected great compassion! As you now first appear to illuminate Jambudvīpa, may your great mercy protect me. You should announce this to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja: 'I pray that you will show me the skillful means within a dream so that I may confess and repent for having committed root transgressions, and thereby attain the eye of wisdom regarding the skillful means of the Mahāyāna.'"

“Good son! When that bodhisattva who has first resolved [for awakening] is in a dream at the appearance of the dawn light, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja manifests a body to him according to his needs. Through various skillful means, he causes that bodhisattva who has first resolved to confess and repent for all previously committed offenses. He reveals the wisdom of skillful means to cause that bodhisattva to feel deep trepidation, so that he may attain the samādhi of non-forgetfulness regarding the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, firmly abide in the Mahāyāna, swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās, and before long achieve all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).”
"Furthermore, good son! A bodhisattva who has first resolved on awakening says to another person:
'You are currently unable to take delight in the Mahāyāna, nor can you practice the six pāramitās; ultimately, you will never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"It would be better to immediately give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha and swiftly bring an end to birth and death by entering parinirvāṇa.
The rest is as explained above.
This is called the second root grave offense committed by a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind on enlightenment.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening says to another person:
'What use have you now for receiving and training in the Prātimokṣa discipline?'"

You should swiftly resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, uphold and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras, and purify all unwholesome actions previously committed through body, speech, and mind, so that you do not undergo the retribution of future evil fruits.
The remainder is as explained above.
This is called the third root grave offense committed by a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment].
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind says to others:

"You should not now listen to, receive, read, or recite the sūtras of the śrāvakas; you should rather conceal the sūtras of the śrāvakas, for within the teachings of the śrāvakas there is no great fruit or reward, and they cannot sever the fetters and afflictions."
You should listen to, receive, read, and recite this pure and profound Mahāyāna sūtra; it can eliminate all unwholesome karma and enable you to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Once these words have been spoken, both the one who utters them and the one who accepts them with faith are said to have committed a root offense.
The rest is as explained above.
This is called the fourth root heavy offense committed by a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment].
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment may be deceitful and divisive, seeking fame, gain, and honor; he praises Mahāyāna sūtras and explains them to others, yet says to people:
'I am one who thoroughly understands the Mahāyāna.'"

For the sake of greed for profit, upon seeing others who explain Mahāyāna sūtras receiving offerings, they harbor hatred, disparage, and treat them with contempt; being self-conceited, they utter false and deceptive words, claiming to have attained superhuman states.
One who performs this practice abandons the state of security and commits a *pārājika* offense; within the Mahāyāna, it constitutes the gravest root transgression.
O son of good family!

It is like a person who, wishing to go to an island of jewels, boards a ship and enters the sea; yet on the way, he destroys his own vessel, drowns and dies, and failing to save his own life, how could he ever obtain the jewels?

It is just like a bodhisattva who has first resolved on enlightenment: having boarded the ship of right faith to enter the deep and vast ocean of the Mahāyāna Dharma, he has only just entered the sea when he destroys his own ship of faith and loses the life-force of wisdom.

Thus, a foolish bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment, out of envy, utters false and deceptive words claiming to have attained superhuman states, thereby committing a grave root offense against the Mahāyāna.
The rest is as explained above.
This is called the bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening committing the fifth root grave offense.
Furthermore, good son!
In future ages, bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds will say to other bodhisattvas, whether householders or renunciants who have likewise first resolved their minds:

"The profound meaning of emptiness within the sūtras, as well as the various adornments of samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and the stages of patience—these are the objects of contemplation and practice for the great, wise bodhisattvas. One should receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras, and furthermore, analyze and expound them for others."

I have understood this for myself and speak it for you out of compassion; you, too, should act according to what has been taught, so that you may attain knowledge and vision regarding the profound and wondrous Dharma.

That bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind does not say, "I have read, recited, contemplated, and understood through hearing from others," but rather claims it was attained by themselves. All such instances are due to the causes and conditions of greedily seeking gain and offerings, whereby they flatter themselves; they betray the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all worthy sages of the three periods of time, commit the most profound and grave offenses against the Mahāyāna, and lose the path of humans and devas.
If one cannot even attain the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, by what means could one gradually progress to reach the Mahāyāna?
Good son! It is like a man who leads a multitude of people through a vast wilderness; as they pass through a dense forest, they become extremely hungry and thirsty.
Seeing various beautiful fruits in that forest, he abandoned them and took poisonous fruit instead; having eaten it, his life came to an end.
Noble son! If even that person was unable to save himself, how much less could he possibly deliver others?

It is the same for that bodhisattva who has first resolved on enlightenment: having now obtained this human body which is so difficult to find, and having encountered a virtuous friend to give rise to the mind of the Great Vehicle, he yet craves gain and offerings and lightly sells himself. He commits a grave root offense, violating and betraying the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time, and is abandoned by all the worthy sages, falling into the evil realms.
Therefore, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras should not associate with such evil bodhisattvas; if they do so, they too will all incur transgression.
The remainder is as explained above.
This is called the first bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon awakening committing the sixth root grave offense.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

In the evil world of the future, bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds will engage in various kinds of outcaste (caṇḍāla) conduct, namely: the kṣatriya outcaste, the brāhmaṇa outcaste, the minister outcaste, the great general outcaste, the vaiśya outcaste, and the śūdra outcaste.
What is meant by the term "caṇḍāla"?
It refers to those who perform various evil mental actions.

Such evil bhikṣus claim for themselves wisdom, rely on their own wealth and treasures to practice giving, and are negligent, arrogant, resentful, and envious toward other virtuous bhikṣus, engaging with them in mutual strife and contention.
Relying on the power of the king’s ministers, they seized the property of virtuous bhikṣus to present to the great ministers; once the ministers had received it, they passed it on to the king.
It was the same with the property of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"Good son! The king, the great ministers, and the evil bhikṣus committed root offenses.
The rest is as explained above."
This is called the first bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment committing the seventh root grave offense.

Furthermore, son of good family, in the evil world of the future, bodhisattvas who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment will engage in various kinds of *caṇḍāla* conduct, namely: the *kṣatriya-caṇḍāla*, the *brāhmaṇa-caṇḍāla*, the minister-*caṇḍāla*, the great general-*caṇḍāla*, the vaiśya-*caṇḍāla*, and the śūdra-*caṇḍāla*.

These evil bhikṣus rely on the power of kings and great ministers; they claim to possess wisdom and, relying on their own wealth and treasures, practice giving. They treat virtuous bhikṣus with contempt and derision, engaging in strife and causing them distress. They proclaim what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and what is the Dharma as not the Dharma. They abandon the authentic sūtras and vinaya, propounding inverted interpretations. They sever the study of Prajñāpāramitā and depart from the mind of compassion. Disbelieving the sūtras and skillful means precepts taught by the Tathāgata, they establish regulations that violate the Dharma. They cause pure bhikṣus of virtuous conduct to cease their seated meditation and recitation of the sūtras; they inflict suffering upon those who were previously free from it, and cause the suffering of those already afflicted to increase further.

Constantly harboring an evil mind, they destroy virtuous deportment; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they have no sense of proper timing, violating prohibitions and breaking the precepts. In truth they are not śramaṇas, yet they claim to be śramaṇas; in truth they do not practice the Brahma-faring, yet they call themselves practitioners of the Brahma-faring. Not understanding the sūtras and treatises themselves, they explain them to others, seeking to draw in the fourfold assembly for offerings and veneration.
"Good son! The king, the great ministers, and the wicked bhikṣus have committed root offenses.
The rest is as explained above."
This is called the eighth root grave offense committed by a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind on enlightenment. "Good son!

Those good bhikṣus who practice dhyāna and recite the sūtras are all practicing the direct cause for the transcendence of the Buddha-dharma; they are supreme fields of merit, and they are vessels for the samādhi of patience. They are able to preach the wondrous Dharma to bring sentient beings to fulfillment, shatter the darkness of ignorance, open the eyes of the world, and rescue sentient beings from the evils of afflictions and karma."
If they cause such disturbance, they commit a grave offense.
These sons of good family who have committed the eight root grave offenses have not yet deeply entered the Buddha’s true Dharma, because their merit and wisdom are extremely meager.

"Good son! Once a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind upon awakening commits these eight root grave offenses, all the roots of goodness previously cultivated will be utterly consumed by fire. Having committed a *pārājika* offense, they depart from the state of peace and security; they lose the bliss of humans and devas as well as the bliss of the Mahāyāna realm; they destroy the bodhicitta and fall into the evil destinies, wandering through birth and death, separated from virtuous friends."

"Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha manifests in various forms to take birth in that land; he may manifest in the form of a Kṣatriya, or the form of a Brāhmaṇa, or the form of a Śrāvaka, or the form of a Pratyekabuddha, even down to the forms of boys and girls. He appears before those bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment but have committed offenses, preaching the Dharma to them so that they give rise to shame and feel extreme alarm and dread, and further instructing them to confess and repent in order to eliminate their transgressions."

By means of skillful expedients, they reveal the stages of samādhi, dhāraṇī, and patience within the profound, unsurpassed, and truly correct Mahāyāna practice; they cause one to abandon all evil destinies, attain the non-retrogressive mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and diligently cultivate the six *pāramitās* until their power becomes as firm and solid as a vajra, even swiftly attaining unsurpassed enlightenment.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha does not manifest his body before that person to instruct them on confession, then that bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind should, during the final watch of the night, join their palms with a sincere heart and face the east. They should burn solid black aloeswood and tagara incense and address the Morning Star, saying:
"Morning Star, Morning Star, you who have perfected great compassion!"

Now that you have first appeared to illuminate Jambudvīpa, may your great compassion protect me. Please speak on my behalf to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, entreating him to show me the skillful means within a dream so that I may confess and repent for the root transgressions I have committed, and thereby attain the eye of wisdom regarding the skillful means of the Mahāyāna.

"Good son! When that Bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment sees the appearance of the dawn light within a dream, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja will manifest his body to him according to what is appropriate. Through various skillful means, he causes that Bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment to feel deep trepidation regarding the transgressions he has committed. He reveals the wisdom of skillful means to cause that Bodhisattva to confess and repent, so that he may attain the samādhi of non-forgetfulness regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, dwell firmly in the Mahāyāna, swiftly fulfill the six *pāramitās*, and before long achieve all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)."

"Good son! Because that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha is valiantly intent on benefiting all sentient beings, he possesses such a wish-fulfilling jewel upon his crown, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Śakrābhilagna jewels, which is not shared by any other bodhisattvas."
“Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has accomplished such inconceivable skillful means and wisdom.
Furthermore, good son!”

If there are sentient beings who hear the name of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, or who fashion his image, or provide him with offerings, such persons will, in this present life, be free from all calamities and afflictions: water cannot drown them, fire cannot burn them, blades cannot wound them, and poisons cannot affect them. Neither humans nor non-humans can cause them harm. Furthermore, they shall suffer neither the pains of imprisonment, thieves, enemies, various evils, diseases, hunger, nor thirst; for as long as their lifespan lasts, they shall certainly not meet an untimely death.

At the time of death, the eyes do not see forms, the ears do not hear sounds, the nose does not smell odors, the tongue does not perceive tastes, and the body does not feel touch; the hands, feet, and various sense faculties can no longer function, leaving only a subtle consciousness and the warmth of the body.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha manifested his body in accordance with the deities worshipped by those sentient beings—whether as the body of a Cakravartin King, or as the body of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, or Vaiśravaṇa, or Virūḍhaka, or Virūpākṣa, or as the body of other devas; or as the bodies of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—and stood before those people, speaking these verses:
“The meaning of the Four Noble Truths should be contemplated by the wise; if one understands them, one can leave birth and death behind.”

"Good son! At the time when those sentient beings are approaching the end of their lives, they see the deity they previously served and hear him recite such essential verses for them. After their death, they do not fall into the evil realms; by the power of this, they swiftly escape birth and death."
Furthermore, son of good family!

If there are sentient beings whose minds delight in the Buddha-dharma, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja will manifest in the form of a Buddha at the time of their death and speak these verses for them:
“The wisdom of the Buddha is true; it delivers one across the ocean of birth and death. Quickly seek the wisdom of the Buddha!”
"One shall attain the exhaustion of all suffering. "Good son!

At that time, those sentient beings, having seen the Buddha’s body and heard this verse, contemplate it with a sincere heart; they leap for joy, unable to restrain themselves. After their lives end, they are reborn in a pure land, never again to dwell in the world of the five turbidities. They will always have the opportunity to draw near to that Buddha-Tathāgata and hear the wondrous Dharma, and before long, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Good son! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha, according to those sentient beings at the time of their death, universally manifests whatever sublime Dharma they should hear and whatever Saṃgha they should see."
"Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has accomplished such inconceivable skillful means and wisdom.
Furthermore, good son!"
